summary: Responses by the author of the mail protocol proposal in RFC 524 to the questions, complaints and suggestions it drew from the network community. It collects them in one place and answers each, and the author invites further discussion.

eli5.summary: Someone suggested a way to send mail. Lots of people had questions, so he wrote one note answering all of them.

questions: how does the mail protocol verify an id
subtitle: James White answers the questions and complaints that his RFC 524 mail protocol proposal drew.

tldr.problem: People in the network community responded to the mail protocol proposed in RFC 524 with questions, complaints and suggestions.
tldr.mechanism: The author collects them in one note, grouped as questions, complaints, suggested additions and meta-comments, and answers each, often agreeing and sometimes pushing back.
tldr.outcome: He invites more discussion and promises to answer further critiques by RFC.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 555 as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It answers comments on RFC 524, including those in RFC 539.

sections.title: Purpose of the Response
sections.content: A number of people responded to the author's mail protocol proposal in RFC 524. This note collects the questions, complaints and suggestions and responds to them. The author intends to critique himself in a forthcoming RFC, hopes the dialog continues, and promises to answer any further critiques by RFC.
sections.eli5: He gathered everyone's comments in one place, and promised to keep answering.

sections.title: Verifying an ID
sections.content:
Answering a question raised in RFC 539, the note says at least one host is assumed to run a mail server that implements the User Verification Function. A server that wants proof of identity can prompt for an ID, contact that verifier with the individual's name and the test Id, and accept or reject the ID command accordingly. The NIC, it says, will provide this service.

Servers are not required to ask for IDs. Those that do not simply treat any ID command as a NOP. An Id is separate from host passwords and has nothing to do with accounting: it exists to stop one person authoring mail and claiming someone else wrote it. Billing, if wanted, uses the USER, PASS and ACCT commands.
sections.eli5: A computer can phone a trusted office to check that the sender is who they say. If a computer does not care, it just skips the check.

sections.title: Complaints and Suggested Additions
sections.content:
On the Telnet Go-Ahead objection the author replies "Agreed. My mistake", and says some other single NVT character could end the two commands (COMMENTS and TEXT) that use <CA2>. He also agrees to the Dynamic, Optional, Static order of parameters, to using the author as the default signature, to warning the server of mail size, to discouraging required logins, and to changing INTERRUPT to URGENT.

He does not agree on numeric levels of urgency, seeing no value unless the protocol says what a server should do for each. On whether the protocol should be a subsystem or a separate RJE-like server, he retracts his own suggestion in favor of Owen's idea of a skeletal Unified User Level Protocol with mail defined as a subsystem, and, after some thought, agrees with Crocker and Postel that their FTP-use approach is better. He also proposes the forwarding reply 476 <localname> -- is his location.
sections.eli5: He said yes to most fixes, said no to ten levels of "urgent", and changed his mind on how mail should use file transfer.

sections.title: A Minimal Implementation
sections.content:
The author apologizes for the size and non-tutorial style of the protocol document, noting that the glossary helped him design it. In answer to a request for minimum implementation subsets, he divides the commands into three groups for a server that only supports delivering mail.

  • Commands that must be implemented, such as MAIL, DELIVER, FILE, LOCATION, TEXT, AUTHOR, RECIPIENT, TITLE, ABORT and EXIT.
  • Commands that can be treated as NOPs, such as ID, SIGNATURE and DISPOSITION.
  • Commands that need not be recognized, such as the DISTRIBUTE, FORWARD, RECORD, RETRIEVE, UPDATE and VERIFY functions.

Such a subset supports all functions of the current FTP mail protocol, makes author and title explicit, lets the text reside at a third host, and permits multiple recipients.
sections.eli5: He showed the smallest set of commands a computer needs to receive mail, and which ones it can safely ignore.
